procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 10.02.2020 of the High Court of Punjab & Haryana at Chandigarh in CRLA No. 398 of 2017
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellants were convicted by the Sessions Court for offences under Sections 364, 302, 120-B, and 201 of the IPC. They appealed to the High Court. The High Court confirmed the appellants’ conviction but acquitted other accused.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellants, whose conviction was confirmed by the High Court, appealed to the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal.

directions: The judgments dated 14th February 2017 and 17th February 2017 passed by the learned Additional Sessions Judge, Ambala in Sessions Case no. 16 of 2013, as well as the impugned judgment dated 10th February 2020 passed in Criminal Appeal Nos. D-335-DB and D-398-DB of 2017 (O&M) by the High Court of Punjab and Haryana at Chandigarh are quashed and set aside.
If appellants are in prison, they shall be immediately set at liberty unless required in connection with any other offence.

issue.issue_text: Whether the conviction and sentence of the appellants under Sections 364, 302, 120-B and 201 of the IPC for abduction and murder were justified.

facts: The appellants were convicted by the Sessions Court and the High Court for abduction, murder, criminal conspiracy, and causing the disappearance of evidence (Sections 364, 302, 120-B, and 201 of the IPC).
The prosecution's case was based on the testimony of an eyewitness (PW-26), CCTV footage, and the discovery of a car and weapon at the instance of the accused under Section 27 of the Evidence Act.
The husband of the eyewitness, who was also allegedly present at the scene, was not examined as a witness by the prosecution.
No Test Identification Parade was conducted for the eyewitness to identify the accused.
law: In a criminal case, the guilt of the accused must be established 'beyond a reasonable doubt'.
The brutality of an offense does not dispense with the legal requirement of proof; a court cannot convict based on moral conviction.
A conviction must be based on legally admissible evidence.
Under Section 27 of the Evidence Act, only the part of an accused's statement that distinctly relates to the discovery of a fact is admissible.
Evidence of discovery or disclosure statements alone is generally insufficient to convict an accused.
The identification of an accused by an eyewitness in court is considered doubtful if a Test Identification Parade was not previously conducted.
application: The Supreme Court found the testimony of the key eyewitness to be unreliable, noting it was 'full of omissions'.
The Court deemed the in-court identification of the appellants by the eyewitness to be 'doubtful' and decided to disregard it due to the absence of a Test Identification Parade.
The Court determined that the only remaining evidence was the discovery of the car and weapon based on the appellants' statements.
Applying the law, the Court held that this evidence of discovery, by itself, was not enough to prove guilt beyond a reasonable doubt.
The Court concluded that there was 'no legal evidence to prove the involvement of the accused' and that the prosecution had failed to meet its burden of proof.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the conviction and sentence, acquitting the appellants. It concluded that the prosecution had failed to establish the appellants' guilt beyond a reasonable doubt, as the eyewitness testimony was unreliable and the evidence of discovery was insufficient on its own to sustain a conviction.

issue.issue_text: Whether an adverse inference should be drawn against the prosecution for withholding the evidence of an eyewitness.

facts: An eyewitness (PW-26) testified in court.
During her cross-examination, she stated that her husband was also an eyewitness to the incident.
She also admitted that her husband was present in the court building during the trial.
The prosecution did not call her husband to testify as a witness.
law: The legal principle applied is that if the prosecution withholds material evidence, such as the testimony of an available eyewitness, a court can draw an adverse inference against the prosecution's case.
application: The Court identified the husband of the testifying eyewitness as another eyewitness to the crime, based on her own testimony.
The Court noted that this second eyewitness was not only available but was physically present at the court.
The prosecution's failure to examine him as a witness was therefore seen as an act of withholding evidence.
By not presenting this witness, the prosecution prevented the court from hearing potentially crucial testimony.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that an adverse inference must be drawn against the prosecution for withholding the evidence of an available eyewitness (the husband).

issue.issue_text: Whether a CD prepared from CCTV footage is admissible in evidence without a certificate under Section 65B of the Evidence Act.

facts: A CD was prepared from CCTV footage of a Bank of Baroda branch by a CCTV engineer (PW-24).
The prosecution failed to produce the mandatory certificate under Section 65B of the Evidence Act for this CD.
The engineer who prepared the CD (PW-24) admitted that it could be edited or tampered with.
Neither the engineer (PW-24) nor the bank manager (PW-1) had actually seen the CCTV footage that was downloaded onto the CD.
The CD did not have any identifying marks, signatures, or stamps from the witnesses or the bank to confirm its authenticity.
law: Under Section 65B of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, a certificate is required for electronic evidence, such as a CD prepared from CCTV footage, to be considered admissible in court.
application: The Court identified the failure to produce the certificate under Section 65B as the most important reason for rejecting the evidence.
The Court's decision was further supported by other serious issues that cast doubt on the CD's authenticity and integrity.
Specifically, no witness could vouch for the contents of the CD, as neither had seen the original footage before it was downloaded.
The lack of any identifying marks and the engineer's admission that the CD could be tampered with further undermined its reliability as evidence.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the CD prepared from the CCTV footage was not admissible in evidence and had to be kept out of consideration. The primary reason was the prosecution's failure to produce the required certificate under Section 65B of the Evidence Act, a conclusion reinforced by significant doubts about the CD's authenticity.

issue.issue_text: Whether a confessional statement made by an accused to a police officer while in custody is admissible in evidence.

facts: A police witness (PW-27) testified in the trial court about confessions allegedly made by the accused while they were in police custody.
The trial judge allowed this testimony and recorded the inadmissible confessional statements as part of the witness's deposition.
law: Section 25 of the Evidence Act, 1872, states that no confession made to a police officer shall be proved against an accused person.
Section 26 of the Evidence Act prohibits proving a confession made by any person while in the custody of a police officer, unless it is made in the immediate presence of a Magistrate.

Section 27 of the Evidence Act provides a limited exception to Sections 25 and 26. It allows for a portion of a statement from an accused in custody to be proved, but only "so much of such information... as relates distinctly to the fact thereby discovered."
application: The Court established that Sections 25 and 26 create a general and complete prohibition on admitting confessions made to police officers, especially while the accused is in custody.
The Court found that the trial judge had completely ignored these sections by allowing the police witness to testify about the accused's confession.

The Court explained that Section 27 is a narrow exception. It does not make the entire confession admissible. Only the specific part of the statement that directly leads to the discovery of a new fact can be proved.

The Court used an example to clarify this: a statement like "I will produce a knife concealed in the roof of my house" is admissible if it leads to the discovery of the knife. However, the additional words "with which I stabbed A" are inadmissible because they are a pure confession and do not relate to the discovery itself.
The Court criticized the trial court for recording the inadmissible confession, warning that this could improperly influence the court's decision.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that a confessional statement made by an accused to a police officer while in custody is inadmissible in evidence. The only exception is the limited portion of the statement that distinctly relates to the discovery of a fact, as permitted under Section 27 of the Evidence Act. The rest of the confession remains inadmissible.

issue.issue_text: Whether a conviction can be sustained solely on the basis of recovery evidence when all the circumstances forming the chain of evidence are not proven.

facts: The prosecution's case against the accused for abduction and murder was based on a chain of circumstantial evidence.
This evidence included an alleged eyewitness, CCTV footage, a confessional statement, and the recovery of items like the car, weapon, and the victim's articles at the instance of the accused.
The court found several key pieces of this evidence to be unreliable or inadmissible.
The CCTV footage was ruled inadmissible because the prosecution failed to produce the required certificate under Section 65B of the Evidence Act.
The testimony of one eyewitness was disbelieved, and an adverse inference was drawn against the prosecution for not examining another available eyewitness.
The confessional statement was also deemed inadmissible as it was made to a police officer while the accused was in custody.
law: In a case based on circumstantial evidence, the prosecution must establish a complete chain of evidence that leaves no reasonable doubt about the accused's guilt.
If even one circumstance or link in the chain is not proven, the prosecution's case fails.
A conviction cannot be based on suspicion, no matter how strong. The gap between 'may be true' and 'must be true' must be covered by clear and cogent evidence.
Confessions made to a police officer while in custody are not admissible in evidence.
application: The Court systematically dismantled the prosecution's chain of evidence. It discarded the CCTV footage, the eyewitness testimony, and the confessional statement for being inadmissible or unreliable.
After removing these crucial links, the only significant evidence remaining was the recovery of certain items at the instance of the accused.
The Court reasoned that with the primary circumstances not being proven, the chain of evidence was fundamentally broken.
It determined that the remaining recovery evidence, in isolation, was not sufficient to prove guilt beyond a reasonable doubt.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that a conviction could not be sustained solely on the basis of recovery evidence because the other crucial circumstances forming the chain of evidence had not been proven. With the CCTV footage, eyewitness account, and confession all discarded, the chain was incomplete. Therefore, the recovery evidence alone was insufficient to establish the guilt of the accused beyond a reasonable doubt, leading to the quashing of the conviction.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the conviction and sentence of the appellants under Sections 364, 302, 120-B and 201 of the IPC for abduction and murder were justified.
appellant_arguments: The conviction is not justified as it is based solely on the evidence of discovery of the car and weapon at the instance of the accused.
There is no other legal evidence on record to support the conviction.
A conviction cannot be based only on discovery or disclosure statements made under Section 27 of the Evidence Act.
respondent_arguments: The conviction is justified based on the testimony of a natural eyewitness (PW-26) who identified the accused in court.
The appellants' guilt is proven by circumstantial evidence.
CCTV footage also proves the complicity of the accused.
The High Court's concurrent judgment of conviction should not be interfered with as the offence was brutal and gruesome.

arguments.issue_text: Whether an adverse inference should be drawn against the prosecution for withholding the evidence of an eyewitness.
appellant_arguments: The prosecution's case lacks sufficient legal evidence, implying that an adverse inference should be drawn for not presenting all relevant witnesses.
respondent_arguments: There is no reason to discredit the testimony of the eyewitness (PW-26) who was presented, as she is a natural witness and identified the accused.

appellant_arguments: The appellant's overall argument that there is 'no other legal evidence' implies a challenge to the admissibility of evidence like the CCTV footage on procedural grounds.
respondent_arguments: The CCTV footage proves the complicity of the accused and should be considered as evidence.

appellant_arguments: Statements made under the alleged memorandum under Section 27 of the Evidence Act are not sufficient for conviction, implying the confessional part is inadmissible.

cases.case_name: K. Chinnaswamy Reddy v. State of A.P.
cases.principle: To determine the extent of admissibility of a statement made by an accused under Section 27 of the Evidence Act, specifically distinguishing the part that leads to a discovery from the confessional part.

That under Section 27 of the Evidence Act, the part of an accused's statement that is a confession (e.g., that he had hidden an item) is inadmissible, while the part that leads to the discovery of a fact is admissible.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: For a conviction to be based on circumstantial evidence, the following conditions must be met: (1) The circumstances from which the conclusion of guilt is drawn must be fully established, not merely 'may be' established. (2) The established facts must be consistent only with the hypothesis of the accused's guilt and should not be explainable by any other hypothesis. (3) The circumstances must be of a conclusive nature and tendency. Evidence of discovery or disclosure statements alone is insufficient to convict an accused.
obiter: The accused must be and not merely may be guilty before a court can convict, as the mental distance between ‘may be’ and ‘must be’ is long and divides vague conjectures from sure conclusions.
It is a primary principle that the accused must be and not merely may be guilty before a court can convict.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Court found that the appellants' guilt was not established beyond a reasonable doubt because there was no legally admissible evidence to prove their involvement. The primary eyewitness testimony was deemed doubtful and excluded from consideration due to material omissions and the absence of a test identification parade. Consequently, with the chain of circumstantial evidence broken, the conviction could not be sustained, regardless of the brutal nature of the offence.
legal_tests_applied: The standard for conviction in a case based on circumstantial evidence requires that: (1) the facts established should be consistent only with the hypothesis of the guilt of the accused and not explainable on any other hypothesis; (2) the circumstances should be of a conclusive nature and tendency; and (3) there must be a chain of evidence so complete as not to leave any reasonable ground for the conclusion consistent with the innocence of theaccused and must show that in all human probability the act must have been done by the accused.
The prosecution must prove the guilt of an accused beyond a reasonable doubt on the basis of legally admissible and unimpeachable evidence.
policy_considerations: The brutality of an offence does not dispense with the legal requirement of proof beyond a reasonable doubt.
Courts can convict an accused only if his guilt is proved beyond a reasonable doubt on the basis of legally admissible evidence.
There cannot be a moral conviction; a conviction must be based on unimpeachable evidence presented by the prosecution.
